metaTitle: Mice Control: Seal Up, Trap Up, Clean Up
metaDescription: Mice control in order: seal gaps 1/4 inch and up, set snap traps along walls, clean droppings wet. Plus identification, health risks and US poison rules.
h1: Mice: Identification, Risks, Prevention and Control
dek: A complete reference to the mice found in and around US homes: how to identify them, how fast they breed, what they mean for your health, and the seal up, trap up, clean up sequence the CDC recommends.
excerpt: The complete mouse reference for US homes: identification, breeding, signs, health risks, and the seal up, trap up, clean up control sequence the CDC recommends.

quickAnswer.lead: **Mice control works in a fixed order: seal every opening 1/4 inch or larger, trap the mice already inside with snap traps set along walls, then clean up droppings wet with disinfectant, never by sweeping or vacuuming.** That is the CDC's seal up, trap up, clean up method, and the agency says to [use poison or bait stations only for infestations that persist](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/rodent-control/trap-up.html).
bullets: An adult house mouse is 5 to 7 inches long including its 3- to 4-inch tail and weighs about 1/2 ounce, by University of California figures.
By the same figures, a female can have 5 to 10 litters a year of about 5 or 6 pups each, and the young can breed at 5 to 6 weeks old.
The CDC says a mouse can fit through a hole the width of a pencil, 1/4 inch across.
One house mouse leaves roughly 50 to 75 droppings a day, each 1/8 to 1/4 inch long, according to University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension.
The CDC advises against glue traps and live traps, and against sweeping or vacuuming droppings.
Under EPA rules, consumer mouse poison must be sold as a ready-to-use bait station with block or paste bait, and second-generation anticoagulants are not allowed in consumer products.

body.text: What is the right order for mice control?

Seal up, trap up, clean up: close the entry holes, remove the mice already inside with traps, then disinfect what they left behind. Those are the CDC's three steps for homes, and [University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension's guide to controlling house mice](https://extensionpubs.unl.edu/publication/g1105/html/view), called the Nebraska guide below, describes the same program as sanitation, exclusion and population reduction.

The order is practical. Sealing first means the traps are working on a fixed number of mice, and saving the main cleanup for last means doing it once. The [CDC's trapping page](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/rodent-control/trap-up.html) runs the same way: it says first to check inside and outside the home for how the rodents got in and points to its sealing instructions, then to set traps throughout the home and continue trapping until there are no more rodents.

Sealing, trapping, poison bait and cleanup each have a section below, after the sections on identification and health risks, which tell you which mouse you have and what precautions it calls for. For a walk-through of the whole job, see this [step-by-step plan for getting rid of mice](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-mice-canada), and for the gear involved, the [rodent control product guides](/pest-product-guides/rodent-control) cover traps and baits by type.
What does a mouse look like?

A house mouse (*Mus musculus*) is a small rodent with relatively large ears, small black eyes and a tail that has almost no fur. The [University of California's Pest Notes on the house mouse](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/house-mouse/) puts an adult at 5 to 7 inches long including the 3- to 4-inch tail, about 1/2 ounce in weight, and light brownish to gray in color. The Nebraska guide gives nearly the same picture with slightly wider ranges: 5 1/2 to 7 1/2 inches overall and 1/2 to 1 ounce.

The house mouse is the species both of those guides are written about, and the one this page means unless it says otherwise. Two other mice matter for a different reason: the Nebraska guide identifies deer mice and white-footed mice (*Peromyscus* species) as known carriers of hantavirus. UC IPM (the University of California's Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program) explains how to separate a deer mouse from a house mouse by coat, eyes and tail.

body.text: Telling them apart is worth a minute, because the species changes the health picture. A side-by-side guide to the [types of mice found around US homes](/blog/types-of-mice) adds the white-footed mouse and the voles, shrews and young rats that often get called mice. The [deer mouse profile](/blog/deer-mice) covers that species' range and habits and how to keep it out of cabins and sheds, and a separate page untangles [what people mean by field mice](/blog/field-mice), a loose name that covers more than one animal.

body.text: How fast do mice breed, and how long do they live?

House mice breed quickly: by UC IPM's figures a female may have 5 to 10 litters a year of about 5 or 6 pups each, with the young born 18 to 21 days after conception. Multiply the low and high ends and that is roughly 25 to 60 pups from one female in a year, before any of her daughters start breeding. Nebraska gives the same litter numbers but describes them as what a female can raise in ideal conditions, so the top of the range is a ceiling, not a forecast.

The two guides differ on how soon the young can breed. UC IPM says house mice are sexually mature 5 to 6 weeks after birth, though this can be delayed until as late as 12 weeks; Nebraska says they reach reproductive maturity in 6 to 10 weeks. On either figure, a pup can be breeding within about three months of its own birth. Finding a nest of pups therefore means breeding is already under way indoors, and the guide to [baby mice](/blog/baby-mice) shows what pups look like as they grow, how they differ from baby rats, and how to deal with a nest safely.

A house mouse usually lives 9 to 12 months, according to both guides, and UC IPM notes that some have lived up to 3 years. A short life does not help the homeowner, because litters arrive far faster than old mice die off. The page on [how long mice live](/blog/how-long-do-mice-live) works through that math and explains why waiting out an infestation fails.
What do mice eat, when are they active, and how well do they climb?
Mice are nibblers that eat many small meals from a wide range of foods, move mostly at night, and climb and squeeze well enough to reach most parts of a building.
Feeding

UC IPM reports that house mice eat up to 20 percent of their body weight each day, spread over about 200 small meals a night, and Nebraska puts an adult's intake at only 1/10 ounce a day. Their diet includes cereals, grasses, roots, seeds and even insect larvae, along with food meant for people, pets and livestock. The guide to [what mice eat](/blog/what-do-mice-eat) turns these habits into advice on trap bait and food storage.

House mice do not need to drink water to survive, though UC IPM says they will seek liquids when their food does not supply enough moisture or when they live somewhere hot or dry. Nebraska adds that mice can survive in small areas with limited food and shelter and no water, so cutting off water alone does little.
Activity

House mice are active mostly at night. UC IPM says they can be seen occasionally in daylight and are active at times when food is available; Nebraska says they are most active before dawn and after dusk, which is why it recommends checking traps in the morning. Mice also stay close to home. Nebraska describes them leaving the nest up to 40 times a day but seldom venturing beyond 50 feet from shelter and food, and UC IPM sets the usual limit at 30 feet. The page on [whether mice are nocturnal](/blog/are-mice-nocturnal) explains what a daytime sighting suggests and what the noises in a wall at night usually are.
Climbing, jumping and squeezing

House mice run up any rough vertical surface and travel along wire cables and ropes, both guides report. UC IPM says they can jump up to 12 inches from the floor onto a flat surface; Nebraska gives 10 inches, and adds that a mouse can cross a 3-foot gap and survive a 9-foot drop. On gaps the sources line up closely. The [CDC's seal-up guidance](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/rodent-control/seal-up.html) says a mouse fits through a hole the width of a pencil, 1/4 inch (6 millimeters) in diameter; UC IPM says mice squeeze under gaps 1/4 inch tall and through openings 3/8 inch wide; Nebraska says openings slightly larger than 1/4 inch. Which wall surfaces stop them, and how they reach attics, is covered in [can mice climb walls](/blog/can-mice-climb-walls).
What are the signs of a mouse infestation?

Look for droppings, fresh gnaw marks, tracks, nests of shredded material, a musky odor and scratching sounds; UC IPM names the first three as the markers of where mice are active. Nebraska describes house mouse droppings as 1/8 to 1/4 inch long, usually black, with one or both ends narrowing to a point, and estimates that one mouse deposits 50 to 75 pellets a day as it explores. Because mice leave them as they travel, the droppings usually do not collect in piles.

items: **Gnawing.** Fresh gnaw marks are about 1/32 inch wide, and mice typically cut clean holes about 1 1/2 inches across in cardboard and similar packaging, according to Nebraska.
**Nests.** UC IPM says to look behind boxes, in drawers, in garages and around woodpiles for nests made of finely shredded paper or other fibrous material.
**Odor.** Nebraska says a musky odor can occur where house mice have been present for a long time.
**Sounds.** Nebraska lists scratching and squeaking from ceilings and walls.
**Sightings.** Mice may be seen on their nighttime travels or, less often, in daylight.

body.text: A dedicated page shows [what mouse droppings look like](/blog/what-does-mouse-poop-look-like-canada), including size, shape and how to tell fresh from old. Not every dark speck comes from a rodent, though. If what you find is much smaller than 1/8 inch, or sits on bedding, compare it with the signs described in the [cockroach reference](/learn/cockroaches) and the [bed bug reference](/learn/bed-bugs) before you set mouse traps.

body.text: Are mice a health risk?

Yes. Mice spread disease through their urine, droppings, saliva and nesting material, and the two infections the CDC pages cited here describe are hantavirus, spread mainly by deer mice, and lymphocytic choriomeningitis (LCM), spread by house mice. The extension guides add Salmonella contamination of food and allergens in mouse urine.
Hantavirus

The [CDC's hantavirus overview](https://www.cdc.gov/hantavirus/about/index.html) says people get hantavirus from contact with rodents such as rats and mice, especially through exposure to their urine, droppings and saliva; a bite or scratch can also spread it, but rarely. In the United States the most common hantavirus that causes hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) is spread by the deer mouse. Symptoms usually begin 1 to 8 weeks after contact with an infected rodent: fatigue, fever and muscle aches in the thighs, hips and back, followed 4 to 10 days later by coughing and shortness of breath. The CDC reports that 38 percent of people who develop respiratory symptoms may die, and that there is no specific treatment, only supportive care.

The species difference matters here. The Nebraska guide names deer mice and white-footed mice as the known hantavirus carriers, calls for added protective measures during cleanup wherever they have been identified, and states that house mice are not known to be carriers of hantavirus. UC IPM's list of house mouse diseases does not include it either. If you are not sure which mouse left the mess, use the CDC cleanup method described below; it is the same for any rodent.
Lymphocytic choriomeningitis (LCM)

LCM is a viral disease spread by the common house mouse, according to the [CDC's page on lymphocytic choriomeningitis](https://www.cdc.gov/lymphocytic-choriomeningitis/about/index.html). People are infected through exposure to fresh urine, droppings, saliva or nesting materials from infected rodents, and UC IPM cites an estimate that 5 percent of house mice across the United States carry the virus and can transmit it. Signs appear about 8 to 13 days after infection, beginning with fever, fatigue, muscle aches, headache, nausea and vomiting. After a few days of recovery, a second and more serious phase affecting the brain and spinal cord may follow. The CDC says less than 1 percent of people die of the disease and that those who develop neurological symptoms need hospital care.

Pregnancy is the special concern. The CDC states that infection in the first trimester may result in miscarriage and that infection in the second and third trimesters can cause serious birth defects. Pet rodents are a second route: hamsters can spread LCM if they were infected in their colonies or by wild mice, which is one more reason to keep wild mice away from pet rodents and their food.
Salmonella, allergens and gnawing damage

Both extension guides list Salmonella among the things house mice spread. UC IPM says mice carry diseases such as leptospirosis, salmonella and LCM and leave feces in stored food, making it unsafe to eat; Nebraska names salmonellosis. Neither gives a figure for how often a household infestation leads to illness. Mouse urine is also a major source of allergens, and UC IPM reports that exposure to its proteins has been linked to early onset of asthma in sensitive children. Beyond health, mice gnaw electrical wires, appliance cords and gas lines, and UC IPM notes that many fires of unknown origin are believed to be caused by rodents gnawing on wires.

body.title: When to get medical advice
body.text: See a healthcare provider promptly if you develop fever, muscle aches or trouble breathing after contact with mice or their droppings, and mention the rodent exposure; the CDC says to see a physician immediately if you suspect hantavirus disease. This page reports what public health and university sources say and cannot diagnose anyone.
How do mice get into a house?

Through any opening about 1/4 inch or larger, from the foundation to the roof. Outdoors, the CDC says to check the roof at the rafters, gables, eaves and soffits; around windows and doors, especially those without weather stripping; between the foundation and the ground; around attic and crawl space vents; and at the holes for electrical, plumbing, cable and gas lines. Indoors it points to the areas inside, under and behind kitchen cabinets, closet floor corners, the fireplace, the pipes under sinks and washing machines, water heater and furnace lines, floor and dryer vents, floor drains, the attic, and the basement or crawl space.

Timing follows the weather. UC IPM says that where house mice live outdoors, they frequently enter homes in autumn when nighttime temperatures become colder, which makes late summer the time to inspect and seal; a separate guide covers [keeping mice out of the house before winter](/blog/how-to-keep-mice-out-of-your-house-winter). The CDC says to seal outbuildings and garages as well, and another page covers [sealing the corner gaps of a garage door](/blog/mouse-proof-garage-door-seal-canada). Vehicles count too: the CDC's cleanup page notes that rodents may build nests in cars, trucks, campers and other vehicles, especially ones that are used infrequently, the subject of [keeping mice out of a car](/blog/how-to-keep-mice-out-of-your-car).

body.text: How do you seal mice out of a house?

Close every opening 1/4 inch or larger, the threshold the Nebraska guide sets, with something a mouse cannot chew through. The CDC's instruction is to fill small holes with steel wool and hold it in place with caulk or spray foam, and to fix larger holes with lath screen or lath metal, cement, hardware cloth or metal sheeting. It also says to fix gaps in trailer skirting and to use flashing around the base of the house.

body.text: The sources differ on two materials. UC IPM calls steel wool pads a good temporary plug that may rust over time, and it lists insulating (expanding) foam among the gnawable materials that are unsuitable for plugging mouse holes, while the CDC allows spray foam as a way to hold steel wool in place. Read together, foam secures the metal; it is not the barrier. Wood is the other: Nebraska accepts it for larger openings but rules out boards less than 1/2 inch thick, and UC IPM lists wood as gnawable. Which grade to use, how to pack it and when copper mesh is the better choice are covered in [steel wool for mice](/blog/steel-wool-for-mice).
Remove food and shelter while you seal

Sanitation will not end an infestation, but it makes the other steps work. Nebraska calls total elimination through sanitation alone almost impossible, and UC IPM says good sanitation will seldom completely control house mice, while poor sanitation attracts them and lets them thrive in greater numbers. The CDC's seal-up page lists the specifics.

items: **Food.** Keep food in thick plastic, metal or glass containers with tight lids, and grains and animal feed in thick plastic or metal ones; clean up spilled food right away and wash dishes and cooking utensils soon after use.
**Pet food.** Put it away after use, and do not leave food or water bowls out overnight.
**Garbage.** Use thick plastic or metal containers with tight lids.
**Bird feeders and compost.** Keep feeders away from the house and fit squirrel guards; keep compost bins at least 100 feet from the house.

**Woodpiles and storage.** Move woodpiles 100 feet or more from the home and raise the wood at least 1 foot off the ground. For stored materials in general, Nebraska advises keeping them, whenever possible, at least 8 inches off the ground and at least 1 foot away from walls.
**Vegetation.** Keep grass and shrubbery within 100 feet of the home well trimmed.

body.text: The same habits pay off against other pests. Ants exploit the same crumbs and gaps, and the [ant reference](/learn/ants) covers them. Woodpiles and leaf litter also feature in the [tick control guide](/blog/ultimate-tick-control-guide-ontario), and the tarps, saucers and other yard items that hold standing water are a subject of the [backyard mosquito control guide](/blog/ultimate-backyard-mosquito-control-guide).
Which mouse traps work best, and how do you set them?

Snap traps, set in numbers along walls, are the first choice. The [CDC's trapping guidance](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/rodent-control/trap-up.html) recommends traditional snap traps of the right kind for the animal, since mouse traps and rat traps differ. UC IPM calls trapping a great first step and the preferred method in homes, garages and other structures where only a few mice are present, and notes that it avoids the odor that can follow when poisoned mice die inside a building.

items: **Bait lightly.** The CDC suggests a small amount of chunky peanut butter or mutton fat on the bait pan. UC IPM adds that the best bait is often whatever the mice are already eating, that peanut butter can pose an allergy risk to people in some settings, and that nesting material such as a ball of cotton or dental floss can attract breeding females.
**Set against the wall.** The CDC says to place the trap on the floor with the baited end next to the wall, so that trap and wall form a T, because rodents prefer to run next to walls.

**Use plenty.** UC IPM and Nebraska both say to space traps no more than about 10 feet apart where mice are active. As a rough guide, Nebraska says two dozen properly placed snap traps are enough for a new infestation in a 1,500-square-foot structure, and UC IPM says pairs set 1 to 2 inches apart can increase the catch.

**Cover the quiet areas.** The CDC says to put traps near where rodents seem to be entering, such as attics, basements, crawl spaces and other areas without regular human traffic, and out of reach of children and pets.

**Check daily.** The CDC says to check traps daily, dispose of dead rodents immediately and reset the traps until rodent activity has stopped. Its yardstick for the end of the job is a week with no rodents captured and no new signs of them.

body.caption: The CDC's stated reason for avoiding glue and live traps is that they can scare rodents into urinating, which can raise the chance of getting sick.

body.text: The alternatives to a snap trap are harder on the mouse than they look. UC IPM points out that a mouse stuck to a glue board might not die quickly and will need to be euthanized, and that drowning a trapped mouse is not considered humane. Releasing a live-caught mouse outdoors fails as well: UC IPM cites evidence that house mice moved as much as half a mile from their home range can navigate back to the nest, and it notes that California law makes it illegal to relocate live wildlife, including house mice, away from the property where it was caught without a state permit. The guide to [getting rid of mice humanely](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-mice-humanely) sets out the options that remain.
Each design gets its own section in the full comparison of [mouse trap types](/blog/mice-traps), along with how many to set, where to put them and how to dispose of the catch.
When is mouse poison appropriate, and what are the EPA rules?

Poison bait is a backup, not a first step: the CDC says to use poison or bait stations only for infestations that persist, and recommends EPA-registered products. The drawbacks are specific. UC IPM states that all rodenticides are toxic to people, pets and wildlife, and that because house mice tend to stay within 30 feet of the nest, using a rodenticide will often result in mice dying inside the structure, where the bodies can cause an odor. Nebraska adds that predicting where a poisoned mouse will die is impossible.

Federal rules shape what you can buy. Under the [EPA's restrictions on rodenticide products](https://www.epa.gov/rodenticides/restrictions-rodenticide-products), a consumer product must be a ready-to-use bait station that contains or is packaged with bait in block or paste form; pelleted baits are no longer permitted in products aimed at the consumer market. A consumer package may include up to one pound of bait for filling or refilling the station, and consumer products are labeled for use indoors, or indoors and outdoors within 50 feet of buildings.

Active ingredients
Consumer products

Not allowed in consumer products; sold for professional and agricultural use only

body.caption: Source: US EPA, Restrictions on Rodenticide Products. The EPA page names three rodenticides in currently registered consumer bait stations: bromethalin, chlorophacinone and diphacinone.

body.text: UC IPM's list is different. It says rodenticides sold for residential use are available only in ready-to-use bait stations and names two acute toxins, cholecalciferol and bromethalin, as the active ingredients available, adding that an acute rodenticide can be toxic after a single feeding if a lethal dose is consumed. Neither source explains the mismatch, so check the active ingredient printed on the label of any product you consider.

The second-generation anticoagulants are the group the EPA keeps out of consumer products. The agency explains that they are more likely than first-generation anticoagulants to kill after a single night's feeding and tend to remain in animal tissues longer, so they pose greater risks to nontarget species. Products containing them must be sold in containers of at least 16 pounds when labeled for professional applicators, or at least 8 pounds when labeled for agricultural use, and are not to be sold in consumer outlets such as drug, grocery, hardware and club stores.

For the professional and agricultural products, the EPA says the labels require tamper-resistant bait stations for outdoor, above-ground placements and for any location that children under six, pets or nontarget wildlife can reach. Nebraska recommends putting stations where mouse activity is evident, preferably within 10 feet, and advises against bait around food preparation areas. On antidotes, the Nebraska guide notes that anticoagulants have a known one, vitamin K1, and says no antidotes are available for the non-anticoagulant rodenticides it lists. The ingredient classes, the risks to children, pets and wildlife and what to do after an exposure are covered in [mice poison](/blog/mice-poison).

body.title: The label is the law
body.text: Use a rodenticide only as its label directs, in the bait station it came with, and only in the places the label allows. If a child or pet may have eaten bait, call a poison control center, your doctor or a veterinarian right away and have the product label in hand.
Do mouse repellents work?

There is little evidence that any repellent will clear mice out of a building, and none of the control programs cited here relies on one. On electronic devices the two extension guides are blunt. UC IPM says mice quickly become accustomed to regularly repeated sounds, that ultrasonic sound is directional, does not penetrate behind objects and loses intensity quickly with distance, and that there is little evidence that sound, magnetic or vibrational devices of any kind will drive established mice from buildings or prevent them. Nebraska reaches the same conclusion. The research is reviewed in [do ultrasonic pest repellers work](/blog/ultrasonic-pest-repellers-do-they-work).

Scents are a gap in these sources, not a recommendation. Neither extension guide mentions peppermint oil, mothballs, ammonia or predator scents as a control for house mice, and the CDC's method consists of sealing, trapping and cleaning, with no repellent step. That silence is not proof that odors do nothing, but it does mean no source on this page supports relying on them. The overview of [mouse repellents by type](/blog/mice-repellent) weighs the evidence for each category.

Separate pages go deeper on [peppermint oil for mice](/blog/peppermint-oil-for-mice), on [the smells mice are said to hate](/blog/what-smells-do-mice-hate), and on [whether mothballs keep mice away](/blog/do-mothballs-keep-mice-away), including what a mothball label permits. One branded scent pouch draws enough searches to have its own explainer, [Vamoose for mice](/blog/vamoose-for-mice), and plant-based products in general are examined in [what natural pest control can and cannot do](/blog/natural-pest-control).

Pets are not a control method either. UC IPM says some cats and dogs will catch and kill mice but that there are few situations in which they will sufficiently control a population, and that the presence of predators can make rodents more secretive, giving the false impression that numbers have dropped. Nebraska adds that mice often live in close association with cats and dogs, because the food, water and shelter provided for pets help mice too.
How do you clean up after mice safely?

Wet everything with disinfectant before you touch it, and never sweep or vacuum. The [CDC's rodent cleanup instructions](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/rodent-control/clean-up.html) warn that vacuuming or sweeping urine, droppings or nesting materials can put tiny droplets containing viruses into the air. Use an EPA-registered disinfectant or a freshly made bleach solution of 1.5 cups of household bleach in 1 gallon of water (1 part bleach to 9 parts water).

items: Put on rubber or plastic gloves.
Spray the urine and droppings with the bleach solution or disinfectant until very wet, and let it soak for 5 minutes or as the disinfectant label directs.
Wipe up the urine, droppings and cleaning product with paper towels, and throw the towels into a covered garbage can that is emptied regularly.
Mop or sponge the area with disinfectant.
Wash your gloved hands before taking the gloves off, then wash your bare hands with soap and warm water.

body.text: For a dead mouse or a nest, the steps are the same up to the soak: spray the animal or nest and the area around it, wait 5 minutes, then place it in a plastic bag, knot the bag, put that bag inside a second one and knot it too, and put it in a covered garbage can.

Air the space out before a larger cleanup. For homes and for outbuildings such as cabins, sheds and barns, the CDC's first step is to open all doors and windows for 30 minutes before cleaning and to leave the area while it ventilates. Afterward, disinfect hard surfaces such as countertops, cabinets and drawers, mop floors, shampoo rugs and upholstered furniture with a commercial disinfectant or a commercial-grade steam cleaner, and launder potentially contaminated bedding, clothing and stuffed animals in hot water with detergent. Books and papers that cannot be cleaned with liquid can be left outdoors in sunlight for several hours, or in a rodent-free indoor area for at least three weeks; the CDC strongly suggests six.

Heavy infestations are a different job. For those, and for vacant buildings with large numbers of rodents, the CDC lists coveralls, rubber boots or disposable shoe covers, gloves, protective goggles and a respirator with a HEPA filter, and says workers hired for such a cleanup should contact their local or state health department. Getting mice out of walls, attics and vehicles, finding a dead one by its smell, and what a professional cleanup includes are covered in [mice removal](/blog/mice-removal).
What does mice control cost, and when should you hire an exterminator?

Doing the work yourself costs the price of traps, sealing materials and disinfectant, and what a professional charges depends on what the job includes. This page does not quote prices. The guide to [hiring a mice exterminator](/blog/mice-exterminator) gives a published national price range with its date, breaks it down by inspection, trapping and bait station service, and explains how to check a company's license with your state, while [how much pest control costs](/blog/how-much-is-pest-control) sets mouse work beside other pest services.
The sources cited here name several points at which to bring in a professional.

items: **Trapping has not worked.** The CDC says that if trapping does not resolve the infestation, you could consider a poison bait station or seek professional help.
**Mice are in the ductwork.** The CDC says to contact a professional rodent exterminating service when there is evidence that rodents have accessed heating and cooling ventilation systems.
**You cannot reach the contaminated area.** The CDC suggests contacting a pest control specialist if rodents have gotten into areas that cannot be reached to clean.

**The infestation is heavy.** Large numbers of rodents, or a vacant building full of them, call for the protective equipment described above, and the CDC says to contact your local or state health department if you are concerned about a rodent infestation.

**Consumer products are not enough.** Rodenticides labeled for professional applicators are not sold in consumer stores under the EPA's rules, and Nebraska notes that pest management professionals have access to restricted-use products.

body.text: For a new infestation in a house you can seal yourself, the CDC's three steps use ordinary supplies: snap traps, sealing materials and disinfectant. The guide to [which pest jobs are realistic to do yourself](/blog/diy-pest-control) helps with that call.

faqs.question: Does seeing one mouse mean there are more?
faqs.answer: Often, yes, though no source cited on this page gives a ratio. House mice are active mostly at night and seldom travel more than 30 to 50 feet from the nest, so a mouse seen in the open is usually living close by, and a female can have 5 to 10 litters a year. Treat one sighting as a reason to inspect. Look for droppings 1/8 to 1/4 inch long, fresh gnaw marks and shredded nesting material, and set several snap traps along the walls. What the traps catch over the next few days shows the scale of the problem.

faqs.question: Will mice leave on their own?
faqs.answer: Not while they have food and shelter. A house mouse usually lives 9 to 12 months, but a female can raise 5 to 10 litters of 5 or 6 pups in a year, so the population outlasts any one animal. University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension says total elimination through sanitation alone is almost impossible, because mice can survive in small areas with limited food and shelter and no water. Getting rid of them takes sealing the entry holes and trapping the mice already inside.

faqs.question: What is the best bait for a mouse trap?
faqs.answer: The CDC recommends a small amount of chunky peanut butter or mutton fat on the bait pan. The University of California's IPM program adds that the best bait is often the food the mice are already eating, and that nesting material such as a ball of cotton or dental floss can attract breeding females. Nebraska's list also includes caramel and chocolate. Use only a small amount, as the CDC advises, and choose a bait other than peanut butter if anyone in the home has a peanut allergy.

faqs.question: Can you vacuum mouse droppings?
faqs.answer: No. The CDC says not to vacuum or sweep rodent urine, droppings or nesting materials, because doing so can put tiny droplets containing viruses into the air. Instead, put on rubber or plastic gloves, spray the droppings until very wet with an EPA-registered disinfectant or a fresh solution of 1.5 cups of household bleach in 1 gallon of water, let it soak for 5 minutes, and wipe up with paper towels. Then mop or sponge the area with disinfectant and wash your hands with soap and warm water.

faqs.question: Do house mice carry hantavirus?
faqs.answer: The sources cited on this page tie hantavirus to other species. The CDC says the most common hantavirus that causes hantavirus pulmonary syndrome in the United States is spread by the deer mouse, and University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension names deer mice and white-footed mice as known carriers and says house mice are not known to carry hantavirus. The house mouse is the host of a different virus, lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus, and extension guides also link it to Salmonella. Because droppings from any mouse can carry germs, use the CDC's wet cleanup method whatever the species.

faqs.question: Will a cat get rid of mice?
faqs.answer: Rarely. The University of California's IPM program says some cats and dogs will catch and kill mice, but that there are few situations in which they will sufficiently control a rodent population, and that predators can make rodents more secretive, giving a false impression that the numbers have dropped. University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension adds that mice often live in close association with cats and dogs, because pet food, water and shelter help mice as well. Store pet food in sealed containers and rely on sealing and trapping.

faqs.question: How small a hole can a mouse fit through?
faqs.answer: About 1/4 inch. The CDC says a mouse can fit through a hole the width of a pencil, 1/4 inch or 6 millimeters in diameter. The University of California's IPM program says house mice squeeze under gaps 1/4 inch tall and through openings 3/8 inch wide, and Nebraska's extension guide says to eliminate every opening 1/4 inch or larger. If a pencil fits into a gap around a pipe, vent or door, treat it as a mouse entrance and close it with metal, mortar or steel wool held in place with caulk.

faqs.question: When do mice come into houses?
faqs.answer: Most often in the fall. The University of California's IPM program says that where house mice live outdoors, they frequently enter homes in autumn when nighttime temperatures become colder. That makes late summer the time to inspect the outside of the house: the CDC says to check around doors and windows, between the foundation and the ground, around attic and crawl space vents, and at the holes for electrical, plumbing, cable and gas lines, and to seal garages and outbuildings as well.
